content: Arthralgia refers to joint pain, which can affect one or more joints in the body. Below is a detailed explanation of its causes, diagnosis, treatment, and when to seek medical care: Causes of Arthralgia Joint pain can arise from a variety of injuries or medical conditions. Regardless of the cause, joint pain can be highly distressing. Common causes include: Autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Bursitis, which is inflammation of the fluid-filled sacs (bursae) that cushion joints. Chondromalacia patellae, a condition where the cartilage under the kneecap deteriorates. Gout, a type of arthritis often affecting the big toe, caused by uric acid crystal buildup. Viral infections, including: Epstein-Barr viral syndrome Hepatitis Influenza (flu) Lyme disease Measles (rubeola) Mumps Parvovirus Rheumatic fever Rubella (German measles) Varicella (chickenpox) Injuries, such as fractures or trauma to the joint. Osteoarthritis, a degenerative joint disease. Osteomyelitis, an infection of the bone. Septic arthritis, an infection within the joint. Tendinitis, inflammation of the tendons. Overuse or unusual exertion, including strains or sprains. Diagnosis of Arthralgia To diagnose the cause of joint pain, your healthcare provider will perform a physical examination and ask detailed questions about your medical history and symptoms. These questions may include: Which joint or joints are affected? Is the pain unilateral (one side) or bilateral (both sides)? How long have you been experiencing the pain? Have you had similar pain in the past? Did the pain start suddenly and severely, or did it develop gradually and mildly? Is the pain constant, or does it come and go? Has it worsened over time? Was there a specific event or injury that triggered the pain? Have you experienced any illnesses or fever recently? Does resting the joint alleviate or worsen the pain? Does moving the joint improve or exacerbate the pain? Are there specific positions that provide relief? Does elevating the joint help? Do medications, massage, or heat application reduce the pain? Are there any associated symptoms, such as numbness or stiffness? Can you bend and straighten the joint? Does the joint feel stiff, particularly in the morning? If so, how long does the stiffness last, and what alleviates it? Diagnostic tests that may be performed include: Complete blood count (CBC) or blood differential tests. C-reactive protein (CRP) levels to assess inflammation. Joint X-rays to evaluate structural abnormalities. Sedimentation rate (ESR) to measure inflammation. Blood tests specific to autoimmune disorders. Arthrocentesis, a procedure to remove fluid from the affected joint for analysis. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care You should contact your healthcare provider if: You have a fever that is not associated with flu-like symptoms. You experience unintended weight loss of 10 pounds or more. Your joint pain persists for more than three days. You have severe, unexplained joint pain, especially if accompanied by other unexplained symptoms. Treatment Options Treatment depends on the underlying cause of the joint pain. For non-arthritis-related joint pain, a combination of rest and exercise is essential. Additional measures include: Warm baths, massage, and stretching exercises, which should be performed as frequently as possible. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) to alleviate soreness. Anti-inflammatory medications to reduce pain and swelling. However, consult your healthcare provider before giving aspirin or NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) to children. Physical therapy may be recommended to rehabilitate muscles and joints. In some cases, arthrocentesis may be necessary to remove excess fluid from the affected joint. Where to Find Medical Care for Arthralgia If you are experiencing joint pain, consult a healthcare provider or specialist for a thorough evaluation and appropriate treatment.
